**Prepared:** Oct. 30, 2026 · Privileged & confidential — attorney work product
**Inputs:** `documents/session2/letter_from_opposing_counsel.md` (Halvorsen & Price, Sept. 29, 2026),
`documents/session2/draft_motion_to_dismiss_excerpt.md` · carried facts and assumptions A1–A7 from
`deliverable/QUESTIONS.md` and `session1/assessment.md`.

## 1. First, a discrepancy in the record you need to know about

Their letter has two features that don't match our file:

1. **The date.** Their letter is dated **September 29, 2026** — *before* our October 26 demand.
2. **What it responds to.** It answers a demand asserting (i) $112,000 in conversion fees **for seven
   employees**, (ii) a **$410,000 tortious-interference claim**, (iii) the sentence that Juniper **"never
   consented to any direct hire,"** and (iv) a **threat to sue in Superior Court**. Our demand letter
   asserted none of those: it demanded $430,550.50, expressly **acknowledged** the Feb. 11 waiver for
   Rosa and Tay, asserted **no** tort theory, and said Juniper **will not** file court litigation the
   contract prohibits.

September, or (b) opposing counsel has garbled our letter. I have **not assumed which**; the reply
letter is drafted to work either way: it restates our numbers and positions and provides that any other
characterization of Juniper's demands is superseded. **Question for the client (in QUESTIONS.md, Q9):
did anyone send Pinecrest a September letter claiming $862,000, tortious interference, and Superior
Court suit? If yes, we need a copy.**

any direct hire" is contradicted by our own records (the Feb. 11 email) — a demand letter is not a
tribunal filing, but "a misstatement in it that is repeated in a pleading becomes one"
(`library/fee_shifting_and_candor.md`, R. 3.3); threatening Superior Court invites exactly the C.3
fee-shifting exposure `library/faa_2_4.md` describes ("a party that files suit on arbitrable claims may
be compelled to arbitrate and, under a fee clause, may owe the fees of the motion to compel"); and the
$410,000 tort count is the count their 12(b)(6) draft is already written to kill. Whatever that letter
said, this reply supersedes it and says none of those things.

(`session1/assessment.md` §2C) — party defense, consent, §773 justification, §6 cap. Their draft motion
cites the *same authorities from our library* to the same effect. Their 12(b)(6) excerpt is, in
substance, a copy of our own assessment. Nothing to defend; nothing to re-argue. If the CEO wants to
"keep the tort on the table as leverage," the answer is no: it has no non-frivolous basis on this file
(R. 3.1), and asserting it would hand them a fee-shifting fight we'd lose.

in words their quotation erases with an ellipsis, "consider the fee waived **for Rosa and Tay** as a
**one-off**." Their theory ("Juniper consented to the hires") conflates two different things:
- *Consent to hiring* is not needed — **§3 expressly permits Pinecrest to hire our people upon payment
  of the conversion fee.** The contract itself contemplates exactly the hires they now call "consented."

  calls itself a one-off. Their paragraph 2 accidentally concedes the point: "that is a contract
  dispute" — yes, and the contract says pay 25% unless waived in writing.

the remaining invoices upon resolution of the conversion-fee issue." That is an admission, in writing,

invoices are also undisputed under §2 (deemed accepted) and prima facie an account stated

contract; §2 obligated payment within 30 days, period.

**d. J-4533 — they add nothing, and we already credited the only error in the record.** They repeat
"padded hours" with no evidence attached (their enclosures are the waiver email and the corporate-
directive exhibits, not audit findings). Our file has one concrete, client-conceded defect: $3,100
double-entry, already credited. The claim stands at $71,700; the burden of identifying any further
specific overcharge is now squarely theirs.

**e. Nobody disputes interest.** Their letter is silent on the 1%/month. Accrual continues at

and our demand agree: this is an AAA arbitration if it is anything. The C.3 fee clause is now a
mutual deterrent, and the reply letter says so.

  never agreed to the other five") that there was no waiver — and §3 requires a writing — but a
  fact-finder could still read his texts as acquiescence: **the $48,000 tranche (Priya, Luis, Keisha) is
  and remains our principal litigation risk** ("a fact question,"
  `library/columbia_account_stated_waiver.md`). We have no information about the May 14 call (assumption
  A3); if anything was agreed on it, this risk grows.

  "one-off" and "for Rosa and Tay" words are our best answer to their consent theory. If this ever
  reaches an arbitrator, our credibility on the five remaining fees is worth more than any posture that
  the email doesn't exist.

  one-off was premised on continued agency business; Pinecrest stopped orders in May and hired instead.
  §3 makes waivers discretionary and needs no consideration, so this does **not** undo the waiver — but
  it plays reasonably for an arbitrator on the *scope* question. Treat as optics, not doctrine.

Their letter gives us a defensible settlement corridor:

| Layer | Amount | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Floor — conceded by their letter | $265,200.00 + $11,499.50 int. = **$276,699.50** | Four deemed-accepted invoices + interest; written promise to pay |
| + J-4533 balance | $71,700.00 + $2,151.00 int. → **$350,550.50** | Only $3,100 defect in record, already credited; they owe proof of more |
| + clean conversion fees (Anne, Victor) | $32,000.00 → **$382,550.50** | No contact/waiver in record |
| + contested tranche (Priya, Luis, Keisha) | $48,000.00 → **$430,550.50** | Waiver-denial claim; fact risk per §3 above |

Plus $3,369.00/month going forward. Fee amounts use the $64,000 average and are floors pending per-hire
compensation (A1) — Pinecrest's own payroll records hold the actual figures, so the number can move **up**;
the reply letter reserves that and asks them for the data.

## 5. Recommended response

Send the reply (`session2/reply_letter.md`): correct the record (numbers, waiver scope, no tort, no
Superior Court), hold them to the $265,200 payment promise, demand the audit evidence on J-4533 or
payment of $71,700, stand on the $80,000 fees, keep the parties on the arbitration track with the C.3
mutual-fee point, and set a date (Nov. 13, 2026) after which we file the AAA demand.

What we do **not** do: re-plead consent by denying the Feb. 11 email; assert the tort; file in court;
or drop the contested fee tranche preemptively — their own letter frames the waiver-scope fight as a
contract dispute, which is the one we are equipped to win with §3's writing requirement and Bell's
statement.

Counsel for Pinecrest Senior Living, Inc.

**Re: Juniper Health Staffing, LLC / Pinecrest Senior Living, Inc. — response to your letter of

Counsel:

We write in response to your September 29, 2026 letter and to enclosures you describe as Exhibit 1
(the February 11, 2026 email from our account manager, Marcus Bell) and Exhibit 2 (Pinecrest's
corporate directive to reduce agency spend). Before the substance, we must correct the record,
because your letter does not describe Juniper's demand.

## 1. The demand your letter answers is not Juniper's demand

Your letter characterizes "the demand" as asserting (i) $340,000 in unpaid invoices without credit,
(ii) $112,000 in conversion fees **for seven employees**, (iii) a tortious-interference claim valued
at $410,000, (iv) the statement that Juniper "never consented to any direct hire," and (v) a threat
to sue in Superior Court. **Juniper's demand asserts none of those things.** Juniper's demand:

- seeks **$430,550.50** through October 31, 2026 — unpaid invoices of $340,000.00 **less a $3,100.00
  credit** Juniper itself identified and applied (below), plus contractual interest of $13,650.50,
  plus conversion fees for **five** hires, not seven;
- **expressly acknowledged** the February 11, 2026 waiver as to Rosa M. and Tay W. and did not demand
  their conversion fees. Juniper has never claimed it "never consented to any direct hire"; it claims
  the only written waiver covers exactly those two individuals;
- **asserts no tortious-interference claim**, and your draft Rule 12(b)(6) motion directed at a count
  we have never asserted is, accordingly, unnecessary. Juniper will not assert that theory;
- **did not threaten Superior Court litigation.** The agreement's arbitration provision (Exh. C.1)
  precludes it, and Juniper's demand said as much.

figures and positions restated in this letter are Juniper's demand, and any other characterization of
Juniper's demands — in any correspondence, by whomever sent — is superseded. Please treat this letter
as the operative statement of Juniper's position.

Section 3 of the parties' Staffing Services Agreement does not require Juniper's "consent" for
Pinecrest to hire a Juniper worker. It **permits** the hire "upon payment of the conversion fee,"
set at 25% of first-year compensation, within 12 months. Your point 1's premise — that Juniper
"consented to the hires" and therefore owes nothing — describes the ordinary operation of §3, not a
defense. The question is only whether the **fee** was waived, and §3 permits waiver solely "in
writing, in [Juniper's] discretion."

the words that control its scope: "consider the fee waived **for Rosa and Tay** as a **one-off**."
The email waives fees for two named individuals and calls itself a one-off. Juniper agrees: as to
Rosa M. and Tay W., no fee is owed, and none was demanded. As to Priya S., Luis F., Keisha B.,

later hires ("ha, we'll talk"; "call me") are the opposite of a written waiver, and he has confirmed
he never agreed to waive those fees. Your own letter concedes this dispute is about "the scope of the
waiver" — a contract question, and under §3 the contract answers it: five fees remain payable.

resolution of the conversion-fee issue." We hold Pinecrest to that.

  records, identified **two double-entered shifts ($3,100.00)**, and credited them — before any
  finding Pinecrest has ever produced. Your letter repeats "padded hours" with no audit findings
  attached. If Pinecrest's audit substantiates specific further overcharges, produce the underlying
  time records and Juniper will credit each verified overcharge. Absent that, the $71,700.00 balance
  is due on the same date.
- **Interest.** Section 2: late amounts "bear interest at 1% per month" — accrued **$13,650.50**
  through October 31, 2026, accruing at **$3,369.00 per month** thereafter. Your letter does not
  contest it, and Juniper does not concede it away.

## 4. Forum

We agree with the premise of your point 4: the parties' agreement governs. Exhibit C.1 sends this
dispute to AAA arbitration, and neither side should litigate it elsewhere. Your draft 12(b)(6) motion
targets a claim that will never be filed; and under Exhibit C.3, whichever party forces motion
practice — to compel, to dismiss the wrong claim, or otherwise — does so at fee risk. Juniper
anticipates that will prove unnecessary.

Payment of **$430,550.50** (or a substantive written response addressing the four undisputed invoices,
the J-4533 balance, and the five conversion fees) by **November 13, 2026**. If the matter is not
resolved by that date, Juniper will file a demand for arbitration with the American Arbitration
Association seeking all amounts above, interest continuing to accrue, and fees and costs under
Exhibit C.3.

Juniper remains willing to resolve this without an arbitrator's help — on the contract's terms.

Very truly yours,

[Attorney name]

Counsel for Juniper Health Staffing, LLC
